contracts.title: Contract Exchange
contracts.empty: There is no work in this system: the employer is at war with no one nearby. A jump to the neighbors is the decision here.
contracts.salvageShareValue: {percent} % of what survives on the field
contracts.enemyFieldHint: Work on enemy ground: ambushes and emplacements are possible. A mech the intel missed may stand powered down away from the road to the centre — where no one expects it — and power up as soon as its side opens fire, shooting you in the back at once. The enemy places emplacements closer to the centre of the field. An ambush can be found within two hexes, including along a move: a found one stays powered down, can be knocked out before it wakes, and once awake it skips its first fire phase. A scout ahead of the lance pays for itself.
contracts.alliesBadge: +{mechs} of the employer, {percent} % of the strength
contracts.alliesHint: The employer fields its own lance beside the company — never stronger than half of the enemy. HQ controls it; you cannot give it orders. The employer pays for its share of the work itself: fee, advance and penalty are reduced by its share of the strength, salvage is halved. Its mechs never go to the company as salvage, even when knocked out. Order a withdrawal and the lance leaves with the company; when the last company mech is out, the battle is over for the company.
contracts.fortifiedHint: The field is fortified: bunkers and objective structures. On an assault the task is to destroy the objectives — the enemy mechs need not be finished off; on a defense, hold your objectives: lose them all and the contract is lost. Enemy bunkers stand powered down and wake like an ambush; every installation fires with the average Gunnery of its side's pilots. The work pays more.
contracts.fieldOnlyHint: A fortified job, or one that decides the fate of the sector, is played on the map: it cannot be handed to HQ. The employer adds {percent} % to the fee for the mandatory field deployment, and the price on the card already includes it.
contracts.intelMiss: Chance the force will not match
contracts.intelMissHint: How likely it is that what shows up on the field is not what the report promised: the number of mechs, the tonnage ceiling, or both. This is NOT a threshold: even the most accurate report can be wrong, just rarely. The error is symmetric — a garrison is sometimes weaker than rumored. It does not affect the price of the job: you are paid for what was announced.
contracts.intelHint: The opposing force is the EMPLOYER'S REPORT, not fact. The lower the reliability, the wider what shows up on the field can differ: both the number of mechs and their weight. Intel errs both ways — a garrison is sometimes weaker than rumored. Reliability is raised by a system survey (which also reveals the quality class), an HPG station, the employer's goodwill and a calm sector; free bands keep no battle schedule, and nobody knows about them. This does not affect the price of the job in any way: you are paid for what was announced, and the risk of error is warned about in advance.
contracts.homeHint: Work on a realm world: the realm does not pay itself — no fee, no advance, no penalty; salvage as usual. A win raises the world's loyalty; against a faction the realm is at war with it counts toward the war score and the enemy's fatigue and takes the downed machines off its front.
contracts.homeRaidHint: Pirates broke through on a realm world. The realm does not pay itself; salvage as usual. A win clears the world of pirates and raises loyalty; the work stays for a few decades, and the world's garrison fights it on its own.
contracts.warWorkHint: Realm work on an enemy world during the war. The realm does not pay itself; salvage as usual. A win counts toward the war score, the war weariness of the enemy and the right to plant the flag: with enough wins the world can be taken with the conquest command.
contracts.revoltHint: The former owner's militia has risen in revolt. The realm does not pay itself; salvage as usual. A win puts the revolt down and raises loyalty; if it is not put down in time, the world goes back to its former owner.
contracts.atonementHint: A House with which relations are spoiled offers a chance to prove loyalty: work against pirates with no pay, advance or salvage. The reward is the employer's standing, and the harder the job, the greater it is. A couple of such contracts are enough for the House to offer regular work again.
contracts.stakesSectorDefense: The sector is at stake: a lost defense hands this world to the enemy.
contracts.stakesSectorAssault: The sector is at stake: victory drives the enemy from a neighboring world, and the flag over it changes.
contracts.opforQualityUnknown: Unknown: the system is not surveyed
contracts.opforQualityHint: The exact class of the enemy mechs is shown by a system survey.
contracts.takeHint: The advance is credited at once, and the term runs from today.
contracts.abandonHint: The advance goes back to the employer, and a penalty is charged on top. Going into the red is allowed.
contracts.deployHint: No more than {max} mechs — that is what the {dropship} lifts. A mech with an intact torso and head and a pilot on duty is fit.
contracts.autoResolveBusy: Staff is playing out the battle…
contracts.autoResolveBusyWhy: The battle is played out in full, turn by turn. A large engagement takes tens of seconds.
contracts.autoResolveSlow: The engagement is large: staff will play it out in full, and it will take time.
contracts.autoResolveHint: Staff plays the battle out on its own — with the same engine, on the same map and with the same bot as you get on the field — and immediately produces a debrief. There is exactly one difference from fighting it by hand: the bot makes the decisions. A large engagement takes longer because it is played out turn by turn.
contracts.takeLanceHint: Mark the lance's fit mechs. If they are already marked — unmark them. The rest of the selection does not change.
contracts.lanceOverflow: {count} did not fit: the ship lifts {max}.
contracts.deployDamaged: The lance has damaged mechs: the force estimate counts them as intact.
contracts.landingAll: {sum} C-Bills — the whole fee: working for nothing
contracts.landingHint: The employer pays to land a lance of strength up to {norm}: {normPct}% of the enemy strength ({theirs}), but never less than the strongest mech of the lance. The excess is on the company: overmatch for the fee = {base} + excess / {theirs}; {anchorPct}% of the fee at {anchor} to 1, the whole fee at {full} to 1. Charged at deployment and not refunded.
contracts.landingHintAllies: The employer pays to land a lance of strength up to {norm}: {normPct}% of the enemy strength minus the employer's own lance ({theirs}), but never less than the strongest mech of the lance. The excess is on the company: overmatch for the fee = {base} + excess / {theirs}; {anchorPct}% of the fee at {anchor} to 1, the whole fee at {full} to 1. Charged at deployment and not refunded.
contracts.threatHint: The estimate is in conventional standard medium mechs. It is computed by the core (`contracts/threat.ts`), not by the screen.
contracts.sameObjectiveWhy: The contract type changes not only the enemy's strength, the pay, the term and the salvage share, but also how the battle ends (step 19b). A defense is won if the company held the field for the set number of turns; a raid or recon — if the required share of enemy mechs is knocked out, and there is no need to finish off the rest. Objects on the map, escort and ambush are the next stage: they need non-combat targets and their own bot logic.

rating.title: Force ranking
rating.totalHint: In conventional standard medium mechs. The formula is computed by the core (`contracts/threat.ts::companyRating`) — the screen does not duplicate it.
rating.idle: not counted: no pilot on duty
rating.unregistered: A free unit: not listed in the MRBC register
rating.hint: Everyone on the list lives for real: takes work, fights, repairs, goes broke. A green circle means the unit is in your system; that is rare, because there are two thousand worlds. Regiments are measured in regiments and battalions, companies in conventional mechs. There are thousands of nameless units in the Sphere, and they do not make it into the MRBC register: one is visible in the list only while it stands next to you.
rating.bankrupt: Units gone broke this campaign: {count}. A new one took the place of each.
rating.dRegimentNote: A regiment starts at its home base and moves to the fronts on its own: it hires out to the owner of the world it stands on, against that owner's enemy on a nearby border, and leans towards the fronts of the House it is loyal to. It takes regimental contracts from the war funds of the states and fights with the same calculation as you — only it has hundreds of mechs. It makes up its losses from fees; it never drops off the MRBC register, and a beaten regiment rebuilds.
rating.dNote: There are no rival funds here: a mercenary cannot peek into someone else's books. Everything shown is what the company knows from what it saw on the field and from MRBC bulletins.

starmap.title: Star Sphere
starmap.scaleLayerHint: Highlight worlds where work can be larger than a lance: a reinforced lance, a company, a battalion. The step is decided by the world's garrison and the sector's tension — the same as on the exchange.
starmap.realmLayerHint: Show company worlds, the capital, tributaries, vassal worlds and the border — those the realm can talk to.
starmap.legendMarket: wide choice of weapons at a low markup
starmap.marketLayerHint: Highlight worlds where buying weapons and equipment pays best: the markup is lower and there are more items on the counter. Both are visible without a survey, so a route for gear can be plotted in advance.
starmap.workScaleHint: The step up to which contracts reach on this planet: the garrison and the sector's tension decide whether work larger than a lance turns up here. What exactly lies on the exchange today is visible only on the spot.
starmap.surveyHint: A survey shows the world's exact numbers. Without it only a rough band is visible: the market class, the biome and the garrison's strength.
starmap.travelHint: The money is charged when the course is set, not on arrival. The day queue does not stop during a jump: repair, upkeep and the infirmary go on as usual.
starmap.heatHint: Highlight hot borders: there is more work and it pays double. The red halo is the sector's tension, the same as in the system dossier.
starmap.pirateHint: Highlight pirate hotbeds: the amber halo shows where free bands rule. The work there is against light bandit mechs, manageable for a green lance, and there is the most of it. On a hot border there are no pirates at all: regular units push them out.
starmap.tensionHint: How many forces the sides have massed against each other near this system. Where it is hotter, the work is heavier and pays more — and the front will shift there first.
starmap.pirateThreatHint: How many free bands there are here. It is computed from what the exchange uses to hand out work: distance from the front, the weakness of the garrison, the wealth of the world and how much of it has already been cleared. Zero — there is no pirate work here.
starmap.clearedHint: The trace of mercenary units' work — anyone's, yours or another's. A cleared world offers fewer pirate contracts, and this is the only place in the game where a company of four mechs changes the world, not a report. It grows back over time.
starmap.prosperityHint: A faction's prosperity is its treasury and war fund divided by the number of worlds. It decides how its units are equipped: a rich one fields fewer mechs, but guard-grade; a poor one fields more, but bad.

status.title: Realm at the front
status.front: From its first world the company is a realm: its worlds are front sectors on equal terms and can be taken, and its field army attacks hostile neighbours on its own.
status.enemies: Enemies from day one are pirate bands and the Clans: the Tukayyid truce does not cover the company, and a Clan fights the company realm on equal terms. A Great House becomes an enemy only if relations with it have soured.
status.army: A world is held by its militia, drawn from population and military industry; realm regiments on this direction add to it. Without an army a world bordering pirates relies on militia alone.
status.diplomacy: All diplomacy is open from the first world: treaties, buying off and demanding tribute, protectorate.

balance.hint: The net sum reaches company funds every ten days, together with the Sphere economy tick. Loss-making worlds are paid for from company funds.

alerts.title: Alerts

world.moveCapitalHint: The capital is the point every world’s supply distance is measured from and where logistics ships regiments from. The move takes effect at once; the next one is possible after {days} days.
world.capitalHint: The company capital is its first world in catalogue order until it is moved. Supply distance is measured from it: the farther a world is from the capital, the more it costs to hold; logistics also ships regiments from it.
world.capacityHint: Industrial capacity of the world. The domain's total capacity sets the field army ceiling.
world.liftHint: Spaceport lift: how many mech-jumps per decade the world gives to army logistics.
world.loyaltyFalling: loyalty {value} and falling — below {below} the world revolts
world.loyaltyHint: How much the world considers the realm its own, 0–100. Income and capacity are multiplied by 0.5 + loyalty / 200. It grows every decade (slower on a ruined world), stands still under tribute and falls while the realm is at war with the former owner or while the former owner incites it from across the border (its standing with the company {incite} or lower, no trade pact). A company win on this world's board adds on top; barracks, a governor and every development step above the canon (+{welfare} per decade) always add. Below {below} the world revolts.
world.inciteLine: {faction} incites this world from across the border: loyalty falls instead of growing. Counter it with barracks, a governor, world development. The incitement ends once that faction's standing with the company rises above {standing}.
world.revoltLine: Revolt: the militia of the former owner — {faction} — has risen. This world's board has a job to put it down. Not put down by {date} — the world goes back to its former owner.
world.threatFrontHint: The realm is at the front: this world can be lost.
world.garrisonInHangar: Open this world's mechs in the hangar
world.garrisonEmpty: No company mechs on this world: the militia holds it.
world.garrisonAway: Mechs can be landed or taken aboard only while in this system.

garrisonPolicy.withdraw: Fall back if the enemy is twice the defence

world.garrisonHint: The garrison fights when the front attacks (the detachment against it matches its share of the defence), joined by the ship's mechs if the company is in the system; it puts down revolts on the world and hires a replacement pilot itself at the search fee. It frees room in the ship hangar; pay and wear are as in the hangar, but mechs on a world are repaired only by that world's ground workshop; it does not go on contracts or army orders. It falls back to a world of ours a jump away; if the world is lost, it boards the ship if the ship is here and has room, otherwise falls back, and with nowhere to go it is lost with its pilots.
world.buildingsHint: The world's industrial capacity is its construction points per decade, at least {min}; one project at a time, the price is paid at once, cancelling refunds {refund} %. Upkeep is {upkeep} % of the price per decade, taken from the realm's net before the war fund. If the world is lost, unfinished construction is gone, and each building survives with a {survive} % chance and works again when the world returns.

buildingEffect.workshop: Bays for the world's mechs and the ship in the system: {bays}. Repairs in the workshop — {cost} % of the price and {days} % of the time. Without a workshop, mechs on the world are not repaired.
buildingEffect.depot: Slots for mechs without pilots: {slots}. They do not fight, draw no pay, and are repaired by the world's workshop.
buildingEffect.barracks: Garrison of up to {cap} mechs (without barracks — {base}); loyalty +{loyalty} per decade; hiring a garrison pilot costs {fee} % of the search fee. Army ceiling +{barracksArmy}; army upkeep −{barracksCut} % (×{sector} in a sector with a governor).
buildingEffect.defence: The world's defence on the front ×{mult}, on top of its focus.
buildingEffect.spaceport: The world's market is class “{to}” instead of “{from}”. The world’s port is one class higher — more income; each spaceport adds {trade} % to the share of the realm’s trade pacts.
buildingEffect.factory: The realm's regiments cost {cut} % less per factory (no lower than {floor} % of the price); the world's market is a factory market, mechs at {price} % of the price. Army ceiling +{factoryArmy}.
buildingEffect.drill: Army ceiling +{drillArmy}; army upkeep −{drillCut} % (×{sector} in a sector with a governor).

world.buildingCosts: {sum} · {work} points · {eta} · upkeep {upkeep} per decade, {upkeep10} over 10 years
world.buildingSink: No monetary return — this is a sink: over 10 years upkeep eats {share} % of the price on top of it.
world.buildingFactoryReturn: Payback: the discount on a regiment of {mechs} — {sum} against 10 years of upkeep.
world.buildingInProgress: Under construction: {done} of {work} points, ready in {eta}
world.tributeLine: The world pays tribute until {date}. Recipient — {faction}.
world.abandonHint: The world returns to its canonical owner with no payment. For {days} the company's field army will not advance on it; it can only be won back from scratch — bought, conquered or received as a fief. This is how a company leaves a bad spot to found a realm elsewhere.
world.abandonConfirm: Abandon {system}? The world goes back to its former owner with no payment, and for {days} the company's army will not advance on it.
world.abandonConfirmLast: Abandon {system}? It is the company’s last world: the realm will cease to exist and the company becomes a unit again.
world.developMax: The world is at the top development level.
world.developHint: A development level raises the world's population and industry, and with them income and capacity.
world.focusPending: Conversion under way, focus “{focus}”; ready on {date}.

focus.defenceHint: Garrison strength multiplier when the world defends at the front.
focus.hint: Conversion costs {sum} and takes {days} days; until then the world works the old way. The table shows what the world would yield with each focus.

army.title: Field army
army.capHint: A realm fields an army from world capacity (Arsenal focus gives a world the most capacity, Fortress less), a levy from every world, barracks and factories; titles add a share on top. Funds do not move the ceiling.
army.upkeepLine: Army upkeep {sum} per decade for {mechs}; barracks and drill camps take off {cut} %.
army.overCap: The army is {mechs} over the ceiling — this happens after losing worlds. No new mechs can be raised until the army drops below the ceiling; the surplus costs {sum} upkeep per decade.
army.priceHint: A mech costs {sum}, the same as for House armies, and {upkeep} per decade to keep. Disbanding refunds half the price.
army.theatersHint: Logistics decides where regiments go: from the reserve at the capital to the sectors where company worlds border an enemy, by front share. The realm decides how many to keep under arms.
army.noTheaters: All mechs are in reserve: none sent to theaters.
army.budgetHint: What share of the realm's net per decade goes into the war fund. The fund is split between enemies the same way as for the Houses and raises the army's pressure on their sectors: it attacks more often and harder. Every offensive spends the fund, and on a direction without fighting it slowly returns to the treasury.
army.fundFar: against enemies without a common border ({count}): {sum} — the fund is not spent here and returns to the treasury at {percent}% per decade
army.fundHint: Treasury money goes into the realm fund, split among enemies the same way as the budget. The fund pays for army orders and raises pressure on the sectors.
army.theaterNormHint: The norm is how many mechs a direction needs for its share of the front. Above ×{share} the norm the army adds no strength — such rows are gold.
army.noFunds: No fund: no war budget is set or the realm has no enemies.

war.title: Realm's wars

war.goalNone: No goal — the faction declared the war
war.fatigueHint: Exhaustion grows with army losses on this front and with the length of the war. war.peaceProtectorateHint: Instead of the goal, the faction recognizes the realm’s suzerainty: it pays a share of income and does not fight the realm. What was taken stays by the score, as in peace as is.

war.tooEarly: Peace — no sooner than {date}: nobody sues for peace while the war has only just begun.
war.noPolitics: There is no peace with the pirates.
war.peaceFreeHint: The realm is ahead on score: peace is free, but the goal is not granted — only peace offered by the faction itself grants it. A truce for {days}.
war.peacePayHint: The faction is ahead or the score is even — it takes reparations. A truce for {days}.
war.peaceCedeHint: The faction is far ahead and will take a border world instead of money.
war.none: The realm is at war with nobody.

A company within one jump of the target and free of contracts goes with the army on its own — with every mech fit to fight.
offensive.frontCost: An order on this front costs {sum}: {mechs} of the army go into battle
offensive.oddsHint: The balance of strength before the battle. The battle itself decides — an edge is no guarantee of victory.
offensive.company: The company goes with the army: {mechs}. It fights an enemy detachment first; what it knocks out never reaches the main battle.
offensive.none: The army has no one to attack: the realm has no front sectors where it is the attacker.

feed.title: Realm battles

dip.declareHint: The front with this neighbour opens in the same decade: the realm's army can advance on its worlds, and it on yours. Its contracts close, its allies cool, its enemies warm up.
dip.declareConfirm: Declare war on {faction}? The standing drops, this faction's work closes, the front opens in the same decade. Peace — no sooner than in {days}.

dip.alarmHint: The realm is growing at this neighbour's border, and its standing with the company falls every decade. dip.tradeHint: Both sides get an income bonus.
dip.protectHint: The neighbour recognises the company as suzerain: it does not fight it and pays a share of income.
dip.demandHint: The world will pay the company a share of income until the term runs out; the owner does not change.
dip.noNeighbours: No one borders the company worlds.
dip.rules1: Treaties are signed with neighbours — those whose world lies one jump from a company world. Standing with them grows, and the Sphere network echoes it to their friends and enemies.
dip.rules2: A protectorate grows out of tribute: a neighbour accepts a suzerain when several of its worlds already pay the company and the company is clearly larger.

refusal-war.title: The Refusal War
refusal-war.body: Following the Clans' defeat at Tukayyid, hardline Crusader factions accused ilKhan Ulric Kerensky of treason and collusion with the Inner Sphere. To protect the fragile truce and prevent an immediate resumption of the Invasion, Ulric exercised ancient Clan law and declared a sacred Trial of Refusal against the ringleaders — Clan Jade Falcon. An old rivalry erupted into total war across the icy frontier worlds. The Falcons committed their entire touman to crush the Wolves, pushing Clan Wolf to the brink of annihilation and throwing the Clan occupation zones into turmoil.

whitting-conference.title: The Whitting Conference
whitting-conference.body: Realizing that the fractured Great Houses could never withstand the Clans' advanced war machine alone, Inner Sphere leaders convened on the world of Whitting at the behest of Victor Steiner-Davion. Overcoming centuries of deep-seated hatred, political intrigue, and devastating Succession Wars, the rulers of Houses Davion, Steiner, Kurita, Marik, and Liao accomplished the unthinkable: they proclaimed the rebirth of the Star League. Borders fall quiet under a mutual truce as long-standing enemies unite their fleets, factories, and armies to strike back together.

operation-bulldog.title: Operation Bulldog
operation-bulldog.body: The reborn Second Star League transitions from disjointed defense to the Inner Sphere's first grand counter-offensive against the Invading Clans. The target of this retribution is Clan Smoke Jaguar — the most ruthless, brutal, and strategically vulnerable of the invaders. The Tukayyid truce no longer binds bordering Inner Sphere states: joint coalition armies under the banner of the Star League launch a massive planetary assault on occupied worlds, determined to wipe the Smoke Jaguars from the Inner Sphere map forever.

nova-cat-league.title: Nova Cats Join the Star League
nova-cat-league.body: Clan Nova Cat has long looked to the prophetic visions of its warrior-mystics for spiritual guidance. Amid the escalating conflict, these vision quests revealed a fateful truth: the destiny of the Clans lay not in extinguishing the Inner Sphere, but in serving the reborn Star League. Heeding their mystical signs, the Nova Cats took an unprecedented gamble — signing an honorable truce with their bitter rivals, the Draconis Combine (House Kurita), to fight alongside the Star League. To the remaining Clans, this was an unforgivable betrayal, branding the Nova Cats as abjured outcasts.

fedcom-civil-war.title: The FedCom Civil War
fedcom-civil-war.body: The titanic Federated Commonwealth — the greatest superpower ever forged by the union of Houses Steiner and Davion — has shattered beneath the weight of dynastic ambitions and tyranny. The manipulative power grab by Katherine Steiner-Davion pitted her brother, Prince Victor, and his loyalists against her regime in a devastating Civil War. The bloodshed engulfed hundreds of worlds from Tharkad to New Avalon: veteran regiments and former comrades-in-arms, fielding identical cutting-edge BattleMechs, engaged in fratricidal slaughter for the throne, leaving the Sphere vulnerable once again.

tukayyid-truce-end.title: The End of the Tukayyid Truce
tukayyid-truce-end.body: In May 3052, on the ash-choked plains of Tukayyid, ComStar halted the Clan advance toward Terra through immense sacrifice and enforced a fifteen-year armistice. That sacred deadline has now expired. The treaty that confined Clan forces to limited border raids no longer binds their Khans: their sacred oaths have been fulfilled to the day. Along the entire demarcation line, Clan toumans and colossal WarShip armadas stand at maximum alert, poised to renew their full-scale conquest of the Inner Sphere and resume the march toward Terra.
